sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Limbal Stem Cell Deficiency (LSCD) is a pathological condition characterized by the loss or dysfunction of the limbal epithelial stem cells (LESCs) located in the Palisades of Vogt. This leads to the failure of corneal epithelial maintenance, resulting in 'conjunctivalization' (invasion of conjunctival epithelium onto the cornea), chronic inflammation, neovascularization, and significant visual morbidity. SLET (Simple Limbal Epithelial Transplantation) is a modern, single-stage surgical technique using a small donor biopsy to treat unilateral or asymmetric bilateral LSCD.

sections.title: Classic Ocular Examination Findings
content: Loss of Palisades of Vogt (visible on high-mag slit lamp)
Vortex-like Keratopathy (early sign)
Dull, irregular corneal reflex (epithelial instability)
Stippled Fluorescein staining (late/delayed uptake)
Superficial Neovascularization (pannus)
Persistent Epithelial Defects (PEDs)
Symblepharon or Fornix shortening (in SJS/Chemical)

sections.title: The SLET Surgical Protocol
content: Step 1: Donor Biopsy - 2x2mm strip of limbal tissue from the healthy eye (superior preferred).
Step 2: Recipient Preparation - 360-degree peritomy and excision of the pannus (kerato-epitheliectomy) to reveal bare stroma.
Step 3: Amniotic Membrane (AMT) - Secured over the bare stroma using fibrin glue (epithelial side up).
Step 4: Fragmenting - The 2x2mm donor biopsy is divided into 8 to 15 tiny 'seeds' using Vannas scissors.
Step 5: Seeding - Fragments are placed on the AMT, avoiding the visual axis, and secured with Fibrin Glue (Tisseel).
Step 6: Protection - A large-diameter bandage contact lens (BCL) is applied.

rows: Presence of Goblet cells on cornea (PAS positive)
Thinning of epithelium, loss of limbal crypts
Absence of basal cells/Palisades; presence of goblet cells
Horner-Trantas dots, not total epithelial loss
Decreased sensation, distinct rolled edges of PED

sections.title: Medical Management (Pre-op/Mild)
content: Preservative-free artificial tears (lubrication is vital)
Autologous Serum Eye Drops (20% or 50% concentration)
Therapeutic Scleral Lenses (PROSE/Scleral) to hydrate surface
Topical Cyclosporine/Tacrolimus for inflammation control
Punctal Occlusion

sections.title: RED FLAGS: When to Suspect Total LSCD
content: Chronic Fluorescein staining that never resolves with lubricants
Loss of corneal transparency with recurrent sterile melts
Progression of vascularization toward the visual axis
Failure of standard epithelial healing post-cataract surgery

rows: Simple, low cost, no lab needed
Risk of LSCD in donor eye due to large biopsy

sections.title: Complications of SLET
content: Hemorrhage under the AMT (affects graft take)
Graft displacement (seed loss)
Recurrent Conjunctivalization (incomplete pannus removal)
Secondary Glaucoma (often steroid-induced)
Pyogenic Granuloma at the biopsy site

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: The success of SLET depends on a 'clean' recipient bed—meticulous pannus removal is mandatory.
Always check the donor eye carefully for subclinical LSCD (especially in CL wearers) before taking a biopsy.
SLET is primarily for unilateral cases; for bilateral cases, consider Allo-SLET with systemic immunosuppression.
Recent studies show SLET success rates of >75-80% for long-term corneal stability.

sections.title: Landmark Studies: The Sangwan Series
sections.content: SLET was first described by Dr. Virender Sangwan and colleagues at LV Prasad Eye Institute in 2012. Their multi-center trials demonstrated that SLET is more cost-effective than CLET and safer for the donor eye than CLAU, revolutionizing the treatment of chemical burns in developing nations.

sections.title: Surgical Instrument Checklist
content: 0.12 or Colibri Forceps
Vannas Scissors (sharp for micro-fragmenting)
Crescent blade/64 Beaver blade (for kerato-epitheliectomy)
Tisseel / Fibrin Glue kit
Cryopreserved or Dehydrated Amniotic Membrane
20mm Bandage Contact Lens
